Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
I distract myself with something else
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: For a 64-year-old male politician whose trauma was as a relief worker in a war zone, this self-harm item is the only clearly incoherent element. The rest of the profile depicts classic war-related PTSD with sensory/social triggers, intrusive fragmented memories, and hypervigilant threat monitoring, plus avoidance/emotion-control strategies. In contrast, deliberate physical self-harm as a distraction is not supported by the surrounding pattern: there are no negative appraisal items suggesting self-punishment, shame, or self-directed hostility, and the formulation shows strong Triggers→Maladaptive Strategies links that are better matched by distraction and emotion-control than by self-injury. This item is not impossible, but within this profile it is the one element a clinician would most question as belonging to the same patient formulation.

vignette: Ahmad is a 64-year-old Middle Eastern man who has been a politician for much of his adult life. He was divorced several years ago and has spent most of his time working on political campaigns and relief efforts in war zones. His latest assignment took him to a conflict-ridden area where he witnessed unspeakable horrors, including the burning wreckage of bombed-out buildings and the constant presence of armed military personnel. The trauma of those experiences continues to haunt Ahmad’s daily life. Talking to strangers or hearing discussions about military topics triggers intense flashbacks that transport him back to the war zone. The smell of burnt rubber from a passing car or an unusually quiet street corner can instantly make his heart race and fill him with dread, as if he is on high alert for another attack. Ahmad has developed various strategies to cope with these overwhelming emotions. He tries to control his feelings by maintaining a stoic demeanor at all times, which often leaves him feeling detached from others. When in public settings, such as political rallies or campaign events, the mere mention of military topics sends him into a state of distraction, where he focuses on something else—often work—to keep his mind occupied. The memory of the event itself is fragmented and overwhelming. Ahmad describes how recalling specific moments brings back the same intense terror he felt during those horrific scenes. The memories do not flow smoothly; instead, they come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, making it difficult for him to find peace even when away from the conflict zone. These fragmented memories often lead to heightened threat perceptions, where unusual silence or being alone in his home triggers a constant state of vigilance. He repeatedly checks doors and windows, ensuring everything is locked tight. In crowded public gatherings, Ahmad finds himself constantly scanning the surroundings for signs of danger, feeling as though something terrible could happen at any moment. The cycle becomes particularly vicious when these memories resurface during periods of stress or silence. For instance, after a quiet evening at home, Ahmad might be overcome by overwhelming fear, leading him to recheck his locks multiple times before finally finding some semblance of calm through work or distraction. Ahmad’s attempts to control his emotions often exacerbate the issue. When he throws himself into work, it becomes an obsessive behavior that distracts from his emotional turmoil but also leads to a sense of burnout and isolation. The intensity of his fear responses and avoidance behaviors have strained his relationships with colleagues and friends, who find his preoccupation with threats and constant need for reassurance unsettling. What finally brought Ahmad to seek help was the realization that his coping mechanisms were not sustainable. He found himself becoming increasingly isolated and unable to function effectively either at work or in social settings. The overwhelming fear and memories have taken a toll on both his mental health and his ability to connect with others. Despite these challenges, Ahmad is hopeful for a future where he can regain control over his emotions and live without constant vigilance. The most profound hope that drives him forward is the desire to re-establish meaningful connections with those around him. He longs for a sense of normalcy and peace, free from the haunting memories and intense fear that have come to define his life since the traumatic event in the war zone.
